750.title: Tamar (2 Samuel 13)
750.hook: a king's daughter is violated and silenced; the text names the wrong plainly
750.howItsDone: Jews read the story of Tamar as part of the book of Samuel; some teachers today use it to talk openly about sexual violence and about believing those who come forward.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David rose from the ground after his child died. Your line was I shall go to him. Did you open your hands to something that can't change? A new week begins, and today's story is a hard one. Day seven hundred fifty.

A note before we begin: today's story is about sexual violence. It's told carefully here, without detail, and if you need to stop, that's fine. Tamar is a daughter of King David, the sister of Absalom. Her half-brother Amnon becomes fixated on her. A friend of his, a cousin named Jonadab, hands him a plan: pretend to be sick, and ask the king to send Tamar to cook for you. David sends her. She goes to her brother's house, kneads the dough in front of him, and bakes the cakes. She has no reason to be afraid.
screen: `A KING'S DAUGHTER.` → `A PLAN TO GET HER ALONE.` → `SHE COMES TO COOK.`

segments.voice: Amnon sends everyone out and takes hold of her. And here is the first thing to notice: Tamar speaks. She says no. She says this is not done in Israel, do not do this wanton thing. She asks where she could carry her shame, and what he would become. She even offers a way out: speak to the king, he will not keep me from you. He will not listen. He is stronger than she is, and he forces her. Then, the text says, he hates her, more than he had loved her, and orders her thrown out and the door bolted. Tamar doesn't go quietly. She is wearing the long robe that the king's unmarried daughters wore. She tears it. She puts ashes on her head, lays her hand on it, and goes away crying aloud. That is the second thing to notice: the Bible names this as a wrong. It doesn't blur it or blame her. It gives her words, and it records her grief in public. Then comes the silencing. Absalom finds her and says: hold your peace, my sister, he is your brother, don't take this to heart. And the text says Tamar "remained desolate" in her brother Absalom's house. King David hears all of it and is very angry. The text doesn't say he does anything. Absalom says nothing to Amnon, good or bad, and waits. Much of what follows in David's story grows out of that silence: a murder, a rebellion, a war between father and son. So why is this chapter here at all? Because someone decided her story should be told. In a palace where the powerful wanted it quiet, the text remembers her name, her words, and her torn robe. Her story is told.
screen: `TAMAR SAYS NO.` · `HE FORCES HER, THEN HATES HER.` · `SHE TEARS HER ROBE AND CRIES ALOUD.` · then: `HOLD YOUR PEACE, MY SISTER.` · then, large: `HER STORY IS TOLD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to believe someone who tells you. Settle, and breathe. Think of the people in your life who might one day bring you something painful: a friend, a child, a colleague, a sibling. Picture yourself listening, and leave out what Absalom said. Not hush. Not don't take it to heart. Just: I believe you, and I'm here. Say those words quietly to yourself, so they're ready. And if this story touched something in your own life, you can simply breathe, and know that it deserved to be told too. If you pray, you can remember Tamar and everyone like her. The bell holds the time.
Tamar. A king's daughter who said no, was wronged, and was told to be quiet, and whose story the text refused to drop. Today's word.
Your line: her story is told. Today, if anyone tells you something hard, believe them first and ask questions later. Day seven hundred fifty.

751.title: He stole their hearts (2 Samuel 15:1–6)
751.hook: Absalom wins the people at the gate with flattery
751.howItsDone: Jews read Absalom at the gate as part of the book of Samuel, and later Jewish teaching uses a related phrase, genevat da'at, stealing the mind, for misleading someone.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Tamar, who said no, and was told to hold her peace. Your line was her story is told. Were you ready to believe someone? Today, her brother Absalom stands at the city gate, smiling. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

Early morning, at the gate of Jerusalem. A farmer has walked in from his town with a dispute: a boundary line, a debt, a stolen animal. He has come to the king for judgment. Before he reaches anyone official, a handsome young man steps out from beside the road and calls to him. Where are you from? The farmer tells him. The young man listens to his case and nods. Your matters are good and right, he says. Then he lowers his voice. But there's no one from the king to hear you.
screen: `DAWN AT THE GATE.` → `A MAN WITH A CASE.` → `YOUR MATTERS ARE GOOD AND RIGHT.`

segments.voice: The young man is Absalom. Since Tamar, a lot has happened. He waited, then had Amnon killed, then fled. Years later he was allowed home, and his father kissed him. Now he gets himself a chariot and horses, and fifty men to run ahead of him. And he goes to work at the gate. Notice how the text describes his method. He rises early. He stands beside the road. He asks each person where they're from. He tells every one of them their case is good and right, with only one side of it in front of him. He says the king has no one to listen. Then he sighs out loud: oh, that I were made judge in the land! Anyone with a cause could come to me, and I would give them justice. And when someone bows to him, he won't allow it. He reaches out, takes hold of them, and kisses them. Every move is warm. Every move is aimed. The text sums it up in a phrase: "so Absalom stole the hearts of the men of Israel." The same Hebrew phrase, to steal a heart, appears in Genesis, when Jacob slips away from Laban without telling him, and there it means fooling him. So the line has two edges. Absalom won the people's affection, and he did it by fooling them. Here's what makes flattery so effective in this story. Absalom doesn't lie about everything. Maybe the courts really were slow. Maybe people really did feel unheard. He takes a real grievance and makes himself the answer to it, and he never has to decide a single case. Saying yes to everyone is easy when you never have to rule. The text lets us see it from the side, the way the farmer at the gate can't. A kiss, a nod, a sigh, and a heart, quietly taken.
screen: `A CHARIOT AND FIFTY RUNNERS.` · `YOUR CASE IS GOOD AND RIGHT.` · `OH THAT I WERE MADE JUDGE.` · then, large: `HE STOLE THEIR HEARTS.` · then: `JACOB AND LABAN: THE SAME PHRASE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice flattery. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last few days. Was there a moment when someone told you exactly what you wanted to hear? An ad, a salesperson, a voice online, a friend who agreed a little too fast. Now ask the farmer's question: did they hear the other side? Did they want something? Then turn it around, gently. Was there a moment you said only what someone wanted to hear? No need to judge it. Just see it clearly. If you pray, you can ask for a clear eye. The bell holds the time.
He stole their hearts. Absalom at the gate, telling everyone they were right, until the people were his. Today's word.
Your line: he stole their hearts. Today, when someone tells you you're completely right, ask yourself whether they heard the other side. Day seven hundred fifty-one.

752.title: Up the hill, weeping (2 Samuel 15:30)
752.hook: the fleeing king climbs the Mount of Olives barefoot, head covered
752.howItsDone: Jews read David's flight from Jerusalem as part of the book of Samuel; the heading of Psalm 3 links that psalm to the time David fled from Absalom his son.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Absalom at the gate, telling everyone they were right. Your line was he stole their hearts. Did you notice any flattery? Today, those stolen hearts turn into a revolt, and his father leaves the city on foot. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

A messenger runs into the palace with one sentence: the hearts of the men of Israel are after Absalom. Absalom has had himself proclaimed king in Hebron, and he's coming. David doesn't try to hold the city. He says: arise, let us flee, or none of us will escape him. And so the king of Israel walks out of his own city, his household behind him, crosses the brook Kidron, and starts up the slope on the far side. Not riding. Walking. Barefoot.
screen: `THE HEARTS ARE AFTER ABSALOM.` → `ARISE, LET US FLEE.` → `ACROSS THE KIDRON, ON FOOT.`

segments.voice: The verse is a slow picture. David went up by the ascent of the Mount of Olives, and "wept as he went up". His head was covered. He went barefoot. And all the people with him covered their heads too, and they went up weeping as they went. Covered head and bare feet: some readers see a mourner in them. A king who once danced before the ark with all his might now climbs a hill like a mourner. In Hebrew the verse keeps saying the same two things: going up, weeping. Up and weeping, up and weeping, one step at a time. What's striking is what David does on the way. He doesn't give up. He sends the priests back to the city with the ark: if I find favor in the eyes of the Lord, he says, God will bring me back and let me see it again. And if not, here I am; let God do to me what seems good. Then he hears that Ahithophel, his own wise counselor, has joined Absalom, and he prays a short, practical prayer: turn the counsel of Ahithophel into foolishness. And at the very top, where God was worshipped, a loyal friend named Hushai is waiting for him with his coat torn and earth on his head. David gives him a job. So the climb is two things at once. It is grief, honest and out loud, in front of everyone. And it is still movement. Weeping didn't stop David from walking, and walking didn't stop him weeping. He let the hard day be hard, and he kept going up the hill.
screen: `HEAD COVERED. BAREFOOT.` · then, large: `UP THE HILL, WEEPING.` · then: `IF I FIND FAVOR, HE WILL BRING ME BACK.` · `A FRIEND WAITS AT THE TOP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: walk humbly through a hard day. Settle, and breathe. If your feet are free, press them flat on the floor and feel the ground, the way a barefoot walker would. Bring to mind something heavy you're carrying right now, or one you carried not long ago. You don't need to fix it or pretend it's light. Just name it, and then name the next small step: one email, one call, one meal. Weeping and walking can happen together. If you pray, you can say David's words: here I am. The bell holds the time.
Up the hill. David leaving Jerusalem, climbing the Mount of Olives barefoot, head covered, still moving. Today's word.
Your line: up the hill, weeping. Today, if the day is hard, let it be hard, and take the next step anyway. Day seven hundred fifty-two.

753.title: Let him curse (2 Samuel 16:5–13)
753.hook: Shimei curses the fleeing king; David will not strike back
753.howItsDone: Jews read Shimei's cursing as part of the book of Samuel; the Talmud praises those who are insulted and do not insult back, and David on the road to Bahurim is one picture of that restraint.

segments.voice: Yesterday, David climbed the Mount of Olives, barefoot and head covered. Your line was up the hill, weeping. Did you take a next step on a hard day? Today, on the far side of that hill, someone is waiting with stones. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

Stones. That's the first thing David's people notice at Bahurim: stones flying at them from the hillside. Then the voice. A man named Shimei, son of Gera, from the family of Saul, is walking along the ridge above the road, throwing rocks and dust and shouting. Get out, get out, you man of blood! The Lord has paid you back for all the blood of the house of Saul, whose throne you took. Now the kingdom is your son's. Below him walks the king, his mighty men on his right hand and on his left.
screen: `STONES FROM THE HILLSIDE.` → `SHIMEI OF THE HOUSE OF SAUL.` → `YOU MAN OF BLOOD!`

segments.voice: Abishai, one of David's commanders, has heard enough. Why should this dead dog curse my lord the king? Let me go over and take off his head. And David says no. His answer comes in layers. First: what have I to do with you, sons of Zeruiah? Then: "let him curse", because maybe the Lord has told him to curse David, and who could then ask, why have you done so? Then the line that shows where David's mind really is: my own son, who came from my own body, is hunting for my life. How much more this man from Benjamin? Leave him alone, and let him curse. And finally a hope: maybe the Lord will look on my affliction, and repay me good for his cursing today. So they keep walking. And Shimei keeps pace with them along the hillside, cursing, throwing stones, flinging dust, for as long as the road runs beside the ridge. Notice what David is not saying. He doesn't say Shimei is right, and the narrator doesn't either. But David once heard Thou art the man, and some readers hear that in his answer: a king who knows he isn't innocent. So he lets an insult go by without needing to win it. There's an honest wrinkle, though. Much later, on his deathbed, David tells Solomon not to hold Shimei guiltless. The text keeps that too. The restraint on the road was real. It wasn't the whole of David. That makes the moment more useful, not less. Letting one insult go doesn't require being a saint. It requires one choice, on one road, to keep walking.
screen: `LET ME TAKE OFF HIS HEAD.` · then, large: `LET HIM CURSE.` · then: `MY OWN SON SEEKS MY LIFE.` · `MAYBE THE LORD WILL SEE MY AFFLICTION.` · `LATER, A DEATHBED ORDER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: let one insult go. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a jab that's still in you: a comment in a meeting, a message from a relative, something a stranger shouted. Notice the Abishai in you, the part that wants to go over there and settle it. Thank it, and tell it to put the sword down. You don't have to agree with what was said. You just don't have to answer it. On each breath out, let the words fall behind you like dust on a road. If you pray, you can leave it with God. The bell holds the time.
Let him curse. David's answer when Shimei threw stones and insults and a soldier offered to silence him. Today's word.
Your line: let him curse. Today, when someone takes a shot at you, let one of them go by without a reply. Day seven hundred fifty-three.

754.title: O Absalom, my son (2 Samuel 19:1)
754.hook: the king weeps for the son who rebelled: "would I had died for thee"
754.carry: would I had died for thee
754.tomorrow: The wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:14–22)
754.howItsDone: Jews read David's lament for Absalom as part of the book of Samuel; in Jewish Bibles the cry is the opening verse of chapter 19, while English Bibles that follow the King James numbering place it at the end of chapter 18.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shimei threw stones from the ridge, and David kept walking. Your line was let him curse. Did you let one insult go by? Today, the war with Absalom ends, and the news reaches his father. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

Before the battle, the king stands at the gate as his army marches out, and he gives his commanders one order, loud enough for every soldier to hear: deal gently, for my sake, with the young man, with Absalom. Then he waits. The fighting is in the forest of Ephraim, and the forest, the text says, devours more people than the sword. Then a watchman on the wall sees a runner. Then another. David has only one question for each of them, and it isn't about the battle. Is the young man Absalom safe?
screen: `DEAL GENTLY WITH THE YOUNG MAN.` → `THE FOREST OF EPHRAIM.` → `IS ABSALOM SAFE?`

segments.voice: He wasn't. Riding a mule under the thick branches of a great oak, Absalom's head caught fast in the tree, and the mule went on without him, leaving him hanging between heaven and earth. A soldier saw him and wouldn't touch him, because of the king's order. Joab, David's commander, didn't hesitate. Absalom died there, and they threw him into a pit in the forest and heaped stones over him. The second runner, a Cushite, finally answers the king's question in the gentlest words he can find: may all the king's enemies be as that young man is. And David understands. The verse that follows is all grief. The king is shaken. He goes up to the room over the gate and weeps, and as he goes he says: O my son Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! "would I had died for thee", O Absalom, my son, my son! Over Saul and Jonathan, David made a song, with images and a refrain. Here there is no song. Just a few broken words, and the cry keeps circling back to one of them: my son. This is the son who stole the people's hearts, who drove his father barefoot out of the city, who came after his life. David's grief has no conditions on it. He doesn't say, if only he hadn't rebelled. He doesn't weigh what Absalom deserved. He wishes he had died in his place. The story doesn't let the moment stay private, though. The army's victory turns to mourning, and soldiers slip back into the city like people ashamed after a defeat. Joab comes in and tells the king, bluntly, that he is shaming the men who saved his life. And David gets up and sits in the gate. Both things are in the text: a father's grief that holds nothing back, and a king who still has to face his people.
screen: `CAUGHT IN THE OAK.` · `THE RUNNER'S GENTLE NEWS.` · then, large: `WOULD I HAD DIED FOR THEE.` · then: `MY SON, MY SON.` · `THE KING SITS IN THE GATE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: grieve without conditions. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind a loss you've told yourself you shouldn't feel so much: someone who chose to walk away, a friendship that ended by their doing, a family that never became what you hoped. Notice if your grief keeps adding a but. They chose it, but. I should be over it, but. For a few breaths, drop the but. Just let yourself miss what you miss, with nothing attached. If you pray, you can remember them before God by name. The bell holds the time.
O Absalom. A father's cry over the son who rebelled against him, my son, my son, wishing he had died instead. Today's word.
Your line: would I had died for thee. Today, think of one person you love whose story with you isn't simple, and love them without the but. Day seven hundred fifty-four.

755.title: The wise woman of Abel (2 Samuel 20:14–22)
755.hook: a woman on the wall saves her town with a few wise words
755.carry: one wise voice saves a city
755.howItsDone: Jews read the wise woman of Abel as part of the book of Samuel; some readers set her beside the wise woman of Tekoa in chapter 14, and one midrash identifies her with Serah, the daughter of Asher.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the cry from the room over the gate: my son, my son. Your line was would I had died for thee. Did you love someone without the but? Today, the kingdom is still cracking, and one voice from a town wall saves a town. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

The battering has already started. Absalom is dead, but the kingdom hasn't settled. A man named Sheba son of Bichri has blown a trumpet and shouted: we have no part in David. Joab, back at the head of David's army, has chased him to a walled town called Abel of Beth-maacah. Sheba is inside. Joab's army has thrown up a siege mound against the town, and the soldiers are battering the wall to bring it down. Everyone inside is about to pay for one man. And then, from the top of the wall, a woman calls out.
screen: `WE HAVE NO PART IN DAVID.` → `A SIEGE AT ABEL.` → `A VOICE FROM THE WALL.`

segments.voice: The text calls her a wise woman, and never gives her name. Her first words are simple: hear, hear! Tell Joab to come near, so I can speak with him. And Joab comes. Notice that first move. She doesn't scream at the army or hide in a cellar. She asks for a conversation, with the one person who can stop it. Are you Joab? I am. Then listen to the words of your handmaid. I'm listening. And then she makes her case. First, the town's reputation: in the old days, people used to say, ask counsel at Abel, and so they settled things. This is a town known for talking things through. Second, who she is: one of the peaceable and faithful in Israel. Third, what Joab is about to do: you seek to destroy a city and "a mother in Israel". Why would you swallow up the inheritance of the Lord? Joab answers fast. Far be it from me! It's not about the city. One man, Sheba, has lifted his hand against the king. Hand him over, and I'll leave. She says: his head will be thrown to you over the wall. Then she goes to all the people of the town, the text says, in her wisdom. And they do it. Joab blows the trumpet, and the army goes home. It's a grim ending, and the text doesn't soften it. But look at what one voice did. A whole town was about to fall for one man's rebellion. She found out what the commander actually wanted, named what was at stake, and found the narrow way through. The text records no other voice from that wall. Hers was enough, and a mother in Israel was still standing.
screen: `HEAR, HEAR! TELL JOAB TO COME NEAR.` · `ASK COUNSEL AT ABEL.` · then, large: `A MOTHER IN ISRAEL.` · then: `ONE MAN, NOT THE CITY.` · `ONE WISE VOICE SAVES A CITY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: get ready to speak up to prevent harm. Settle, and breathe. Think of a place where something is heading toward damage: a group chat turning cruel, a family plan that will hurt someone, a decision at work no one is questioning. Ask the wise woman's questions. Who can actually stop this? What do they really want? What's at stake that they might not see? Then shape one sentence you could say, calm and clear. You don't have to say it yet. Just have it ready. If you pray, you can ask for wise words. The bell holds the time.
The wise woman of Abel. An unnamed woman on a town wall who asked for the commander, spoke for her city, and saved it. Today's word.
screen: `THE WISE WOMAN OF ABEL — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: one wise voice saves a city. Today, if you see harm coming, ask to speak with the person who can stop it. Day seven hundred fifty-five.

756.title: David's last words (2 Samuel 23:1–4)
756.hook: one who rules justly is "as the light of the morning"
756.howItsDone: Jews read David's last words as part of the book of Samuel; David is remembered in Jewish tradition as the sweet singer of Israel, and some psalms carry his name in their headings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a woman on the wall of Abel called for the commander and saved her town. Your line was one wise voice saves a city. Did you have a sentence ready? Today, near the end of Samuel, David's own voice, in a poem. Day seven hundred fifty-six.

After everything, the rooftop, the ewe lamb, the child, Tamar, the climb up the Mount of Olives, the cry over the gate, the book gives David a short poem and calls it his last words. It opens like a signature. David the son of Jesse says. The man raised up on high says. The anointed of the God of Jacob. The sweet singer of Israel. Then he says where the words come from: the spirit of the Lord spoke by me, and his word was on my tongue. And what he passes on, at the end of a long and tangled life, is a picture of what a ruler should be.
screen: `AFTER EVERYTHING, A POEM.` → `THE SON OF JESSE SAYS.` → `HIS WORD WAS ON MY TONGUE.`

segments.voice: Here is the picture. The God of Israel said, the Rock of Israel spoke to me: one who rules over people must be just, ruling in the fear of God. And then the image. He shall be "as the light of the morning, when the sun riseth", a morning without clouds, like tender grass springing out of the earth by clear shining after rain. Justice, in this poem, isn't a sword or a gavel. It's daylight. Morning light doesn't choose whose field to shine on. Grass after rain simply grows. Read this way, a fair ruler is a presence that lets everyone underneath grow. Now hold that next to the man saying it. This is the king of the chapters we've just walked through: who took another man's wife, who arranged a death, who heard what was done to his daughter Tamar and, as far as the text says, did nothing, whose own son rose against him. The poem doesn't erase any of that. Set beside that story, it reads as an ideal, and his own life shows how hard it is to reach. The next line can be heard two ways. Some translations have David admit that his house is not so with God. The Jewish translation of 1917 hears a question: is not my house so with God? Either way, the line ends on an everlasting covenant God has made with him. One more honest note: these are called David's last words, yet the opening of the book of Kings records later instructions from David to Solomon. Perhaps they are his last words as a poet, or the book's chosen farewell. Whichever it is, the words the book labels last are not about battles. They are about light.
screen: `RULING JUSTLY, IN THE FEAR OF GOD.` · then, large: `AS THE LIGHT OF THE MORNING.` · then: `GRASS AFTER RAIN.` · `AN IDEAL HE REACHED FOR.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: lead fairly in one small way. Settle, and breathe. You're in charge of something, even if it's small: a household, a team, a classroom, a group chat, a dog. Picture the people in it, one by one. Ask: is there someone the light doesn't reach? Someone who gets less of my patience, less of my attention, less of the benefit of the doubt? Let one name come. Then choose one fair thing you can do for them today. If you pray, you can hold David's picture: the light of the morning. The bell holds the time.
David's last words. A short poem near the end of Samuel: one who rules justly is like morning light and grass after rain. Today's word.

Your line: like the light of morning. Today, be fair to the one person your light usually misses. And look back at this week: her story is told, he stole their hearts, up the hill, weeping, let him curse, would I had died for thee, one wise voice saves a city, and the light of morning. Day seven hundred fifty-six.
